title: Text-to-SQL
summary: A model turns a natural-language question into SQL. It works on small clean schemas and degrades on large, dirty enterprise ones, and its output must be treated as untrusted input to your database.
useIf: Users ask ad hoc questions over structured data, the schema can be curated, and wrong answers are cheap to catch or the data is low risk.
avoidIf: Answers must be exact every time, or the database holds data users must never see and the connection is not locked down.

explain.md: Text-to-SQL looks solved on demos and is not. **BIRD** has 12,751 question and SQL pairs over 95 databases (33.4 GB, 37 domains) with dirty values and external knowledge. ChatGPT reached 40.08% execution accuracy against 92.96% for humans [[r29]]. **Spider 2.0** uses 632 enterprise workflow problems, often over databases with more than 1,000 columns. An o1-preview code agent solved 21.3%, against 91.2% on Spider 1.0 and 73.0% on BIRD [[r30]]. Scores come from the papers and age quickly, but the gap from clean to enterprise schemas is the lesson.

steps.title: Schema linking
steps.md: Pick the relevant tables, columns, descriptions and sampled values. Do not send 1,000 columns.

steps.title: Generate
steps.md: Produce one read-only statement against curated views.

steps.title: Validate
steps.md: Parse it, allow-list tables, reject DDL and DML, add a row limit and timeout.

steps.title: Execute
steps.md: Run under a read-only role with row-level security in the database.

steps.title: Answer
steps.md: Return the result, show the SQL and flag low-confidence cases.

explain.md: **Treat generated SQL as untrusted.** The P2SQL paper shows that unsanitized prompts can drive SQL injection in LangChain-based LLM-integrated web apps, so generated SQL needs the same defences as user-supplied SQL [[r31]]. A prompt that says 'only run SELECT' is not a control. A read-only database role is.

**Row access belongs in the database tier.** SQL Server and Azure SQL row-level security uses filter predicates, which silently filter rows for `SELECT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE`, and block predicates for writes, defined as inline table-valued functions and enforced by a security policy. A middle-tier app can share one database user and set the application user ID in `SESSION_CONTEXT` after connecting. The `@read_only` flag stops the value changing until the connection returns to the pool [[tr2]].

whereToUse: Analyst self-service over a curated reporting schema or semantic layer
Internal data copilots where each answer shows its SQL for review
Exploration tools on read replicas, where a bad query costs time and not data
Natural-language filters that map onto a known set of verified queries

use: The schema is curated: few tables, clear names, descriptions and sampled values
The role is read-only and rows are restricted in the database
Users can see the SQL, and failures are cheap to catch
avoid: Exact financial or legal numbers with no human review
Giving the model write access or an owner-level connection
Pointing it at a raw 1,000-column warehouse with unclear names
flips: Schema grows or turns dirty: add curated views or a semantic layer before widening access
Answers must be exact: switch to verified query templates or stored procedures
Multi-tenant exposure: enforce row-level security in the database, not in the prompt

pitfalls.cause: Wrong join keys, dirty values or business terms the schema does not explain
pitfalls.fix: Link a narrow schema, include descriptions and sampled values, show the SQL and evaluate execution accuracy on your own questions.

pitfalls.symptom: A user sees another tenant's rows
pitfalls.cause: Tenant filtering lived in the prompt, or a pooled connection kept a previous user's session context
pitfalls.fix: Use row-level security in the database, set `SESSION_CONTEXT` per request with `@read_only` and test cross-tenant queries.

pitfalls.symptom: A query locks up the warehouse
pitfalls.cause: No timeout, row limit or cost guard on generated SQL
pitfalls.fix: Enforce a statement timeout and row cap, route to a replica and block unbounded scans.

scenarios.title: Analyst copilot over a huge warehouse
scenarios.situation: Analysts want to ask questions over a warehouse with thousands of columns and inconsistent naming. Users are internal and a human reads results before use.
scenarios.question: How do you scope the assistant?

options.name: Free-form generation over the whole warehouse
options.why: Enterprise-scale schemas are where scores fall hard: 21.3% on Spider 2.0 against 91.2% on Spider 1.0.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable for a small, clean schema or a sandbox for exploration.

options.name: Curated views plus schema linking with descriptions and sampled values
options.why: It shrinks the problem the model sees and fixes meaning in one place.
options.tradeoff: Someone must build and maintain the views.

options.name: Verified templates only
options.why: Accurate for the questions they cover.

flips.if: The schema is small and clean

flips.then: Add verification or move to templates for those questions.

scenarios.takeaway: Curate before you scale: schema size is the biggest accuracy lever.

scenarios.title: Multi-tenant customer assistant
scenarios.situation: A product lets customers ask questions about their own account data in a shared database. A leak across customers would be a serious incident.
unknowns: Does the database support row-level security?
scenarios.question: Where do you enforce tenant isolation?

options.name: A system prompt rule: 'always filter by the caller's tenant id'
options.why: A prompt is not a control, and injected or malformed SQL can omit the filter.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable as a hint layered on top of real enforcement.

options.name: Application appends a WHERE clause to the generated SQL
options.why: Better than the prompt and easy to build.
options.tradeoff: String rewriting is brittle with joins, subqueries and CTEs.

options.name: Row-level security in the database with per-request session context, plus a read-only role
options.why: The database applies the predicate on every access from any tier, so even wrong SQL cannot cross tenants.
options.tradeoff: Needs schema work, predicate performance tuning and care with pooled connections.

flips.if: Each tenant has its own database
flips.then: Connection-level isolation may be simpler than row predicates.
Expose tenant-scoped views or stored procedures instead.

scenarios.takeaway: Enforce who sees which rows where the data lives.

scenarios.title: Exact monthly figures for finance
scenarios.situation: A finance team asks for revenue and margin figures that feed a monthly report. Numbers must match the ledger exactly and be reproducible.
unknowns: How many distinct report shapes exist?
scenarios.question: What do you build?

options.name: Verified query templates or stored procedures, with the model only choosing and filling parameters
options.why: Definitions are fixed and reviewed, so numbers are reproducible and auditable.
options.tradeoff: Coverage is limited to the templates you write.

options.name: Free-form SQL with a result check by the user
options.why: Plausible SQL can return wrong numbers and reviewers miss subtle errors.
options.tradeoff: Fine for exploration where nothing is booked from the output.

options.name: Schema-linked generation over curated views, with SQL shown
options.tradeoff: Still not guaranteed correct, so a finance reviewer must sign off.

flips.then: Offer generated SQL on curated views as an explicit, labelled exploration mode.
Invest in a semantic layer to define metrics once.

scenarios.takeaway: When exactness matters, constrain the model to parameters of verified queries.

quiz.q: Which control stops a generated `DROP TABLE` regardless of what the model writes?
options: An output classifier on the answer text
quiz.explain: Permissions enforced by the database apply to any SQL. A prompt, a classifier on text or temperature can all be bypassed or fail, and P2SQL shows prompts can drive injection.

quiz.q: Order the stages of a defended text-to-SQL path.
quiz.explain: Narrow the schema first, generate, validate and bound the statement, run it with least privilege, then present the result with the SQL so users can check it.

quiz.q: On Spider 2.0 an o1-preview code agent solved 21.3%, against 91.2% on Spider 1.0. How many percentage points lower is Spider 2.0?
quiz.explain: 91.2 minus 21.3 is 69.9 percentage points. The point is that enterprise-scale schemas are much harder than the academic benchmark.

flashcards.back: ChatGPT reached 40.08% execution accuracy against 92.96% for humans, on 12,751 pairs over 95 databases with dirty values.

flashcards.front: Why is a system prompt not a SQL safety control?
flashcards.back: Prompts can be bypassed and P2SQL shows prompts can drive SQL injection. Use a read-only role, validation and database row-level security.

flashcards.front: What is the SESSION_CONTEXT pattern in row-level security?
flashcards.back: The app sets the current user ID after connecting and policies filter rows by it. The `@read_only` flag stops changes until the connection returns to the pool.
